sections.theory:
a. Common System

In this system, monohydric alcohols are named as “alkyl alcohols”. That is alkyl group of the alcohol is named first, which is followed by the word alcohol. For example,

The n-propyl alcohol and isopropyl alcohol are isomers. The four isomeric butyl alcohols are names as follows.

Suffix glycols is used for dihydric alcohols (more commonly for vicinal diols).

The smallest trihydric alcohol is named as glycerol.

b. IUPAC System

In this system alcohols are named as “alkanols”. That is, the final ‘–e’ of the corresponding alkane is replaced by suffix ‘–ol’.

The IUPAC rules are

1. Select the longest continuous carbon chain containing the –OH group(s).

2. The ending “–e” of the corresponding alkane is replaced by suffix “–ol”.

3. Number the chain from one end or the other, so as to give lowest number to the carbon carrying the –OH group.

4. Mention the position of the hydroxyl group by putting its number before the suffix “–ol”.

5. Indicate the position of the other substituents (if any) using the numbers of the carbon atoms, to which they are attached.

6. The substituents, along with their positions, are named in alphabetical order before the parent name.

7. If the number of carbon atoms carrying the hydroxyl group is the same from either side, then number the chain from the end which is heavily substituted.

8. In case of dihydric, trihydric and polyhydric alcohols, the prefix di, tri, tetra etc. is used before “–ol”, along with the numbers of the carbon atoms to which these hydroxyl groups are attached.

9. If more than one hydroxyl groups are attached to the same carbon atom, the number of that carbon atom is repeated.

The following examples will illustrate the above rules.

18.1.2 Physical Properties

Lower alcohols are colourless liquids while alcohols of high molecular mass are solids, at room temperature.

They have characteristic sweet smell.

The melting and boiling points are generally increase with the size of alkyl group, and also number of –OH groups (Table 18.1).

Tidbit

The -e ending of an alkane name is dropped before a suffix beginning with a vowel (-ol) and retained before one beginning with a consonant (-diol).

کمرے کے درجہ حرارت پر کم کاربن والے الکوحلز بے رنگ مائع جبکہ زیادہ سالماتی کمیت والے الکوحلز ٹھوس ہیں۔

ان کی مخصوص میٹھی بو ہوتی ہے۔

نقطۂ پگھلاؤ اور نقطۂ جوش عموماً الکائل گروپ کے حجم اور –OH گروپوں کی تعداد کے ساتھ بڑھتے ہیں (جدول 18.1)۔

مختصر معلومات

الکین (اکیلے بند والے) کے نام کا آخری -e حرفِ علت سے شروع ہونے والے لاحقے (-ol) سے پہلے گرا دیا جاتا ہے اور حرفِ صحیح سے شروع ہونے والے لاحقے (-diol) سے پہلے برقرار رکھا جاتا ہے۔

a. Common System

In this system, monohydric alcohols are named as “alkyl alcohols”. That is alkyl group of the alcohol is named first, which is followed by the word alcohol. For example,

The n-propyl alcohol and isopropyl alcohol are isomers. The four isomeric butyl alcohols are names as follows.

Suffix glycols is used for dihydric alcohols (more commonly for vicinal diols).

The smallest trihydric alcohol is named as glycerol.

b. IUPAC System

In this system alcohols are named as “alkanols”. That is, the final ‘–e’ of the corresponding alkane is replaced by suffix ‘–ol’.

The IUPAC rules are

1. Select the longest continuous carbon chain containing the –OH group(s).

2. The ending “–e” of the corresponding alkane is replaced by suffix “–ol”.

3. Number the chain from one end or the other, so as to give lowest number to the carbon carrying the –OH group.

4. Mention the position of the hydroxyl group by putting its number before the suffix “–ol”.

5. Indicate the position of the other substituents (if any) using the numbers of the carbon atoms, to which they are attached.

6. The substituents, along with their positions, are named in alphabetical order before the parent name.

7. If the number of carbon atoms carrying the hydroxyl group is the same from either side, then number the chain from the end which is heavily substituted.

8. In case of dihydric, trihydric and polyhydric alcohols, the prefix di, tri, tetra etc. is used before “–ol”, along with the numbers of the carbon atoms to which these hydroxyl groups are attached.

9. If more than one hydroxyl groups are attached to the same carbon atom, the number of that carbon atom is repeated.

The following examples will illustrate the above rules.

18.1.2 Physical Properties

Lower alcohols are colourless liquids while alcohols of high molecular mass are solids, at room temperature.

They have characteristic sweet smell.

The melting and boiling points are generally increase with the size of alkyl group, and also number of –OH groups (Table 18.1).

Tidbit

The -e ending of an alkane name is dropped before a suffix beginning with a vowel (-ol) and retained before one beginning with a consonant (-diol).
